title: the DSG techniques of story and campaign design
audit_label: R554 DSG story design techniques audit
audit_comment: The techniques of story and campaign design pins printed pp. 109-112: the chapter head (the story line chosen shapes the gaming environment, three types of adventure design), The Linear Adventure (the certain-order encounters, the dungeon one-route maps, the outdoor thorn-wall obstacles, the no-wasted-design advantage, the high-level-magic difficulty, the tournament fit, the railroad frustration, the illusion of choice), The Open Campaign (the player-choice doctrine, the seeded countryside, the Adventurer fun, the Problem-Solver and Role-Player workload, the world built over time, the story-structure difficulty, the perverse players, the Events technique, the ask-ahead shortcut, the background conflicts), The Matrix Campaign (the goal-driven compromise, the evil-cleric exposition, the guided options, the prepared courses, the expanding branches, the plot events, the soft and hard borders, the multiple paths to the climax, the lost players, the foreshadowed track), the Running the Game head (the two at-table functions), Preparing For Play (the random-generation lists, the coded notes, the THACO shorthand, the map symbols, the anticipated surprises, the treasure decisions), and The Dungeon Master as Master Storyteller (the pace doctrine, the optional systems, the voice - tone, volume, rate - and the word choice and NPC voices).

banner.title: THE DSG TECHNIQUES OF STORY AND CAMPAIGN DESIGN, R554: printed pp. 109-112 - the chapter head (the story line a DM chooses affects the gaming environment he creates; three types of adventure design, each related to plot development); The Linear Adventure (the encounters played in a certain order with little choice between them; the dungeon as the linear setting - the one-route map and the predetermined locations; the outdoor difficulty with the thorn walls and impassable water; the no-wasted-design-time advantage; the difficulty as the PCs gain magical power - the high-level spells defeating the corridors; the tournament fit; the general undesirability - the railroading frustration; the directed play with the illusion of choice); The Open Campaign (the de-emphasized story with the PC choices determining the course; the interesting world to explore; the preparation burden - the detailed countryside seeded with conflicts; the Adventurer fun continuing indefinitely - dungeons, wars, new worlds; the greater Problem-Solver and Role-Player workload - the mental diet, the unique NPCs, the national-scope problems, the nomadic NPCs; the entire world setting built over time; the story-structure difficulty - the players developing it themselves or taking perverse delight in the opposite; the Events technique - the dragon's lair placed in the path with logic; the ask-ahead shortcut; the background conflicts - the wars with the met principals, the endless winter and the man-eating plants as continuing threads); The Matrix Campaign (the detailed story with the player choice; the goal or goals motivating the PCs - the linear-open compromise, the epic and the string of stories; the short exposition opening options - the evil cleric sect with the arrested peasants and the raided temples; the guided options north, east, and south with the headquarters to the west bided; the prepared courses - the raid, the sage interview, the prisoner rescue; the expanding branches steering toward the headquarters climax - the prisoners led as an army, the quest for the item of power; the plot events - the significant NPCs, the visions and dreams, the social changes, the quick scenes; the soft border of the hapless waifs and the stranger's gems; the hard border of the cliff, the sea, the desert, the escalating army, the quest and geas as the last resort; the several approaches to the final encounter, never doomed for a wrong choice; the lost players shown the path gently but firmly - the henchman speaking up, the plain-language sage; the foreshadowed track with the ill omens); the Running the Game head (the second responsibility beginning at the table - the story presented so the PCs are drawn in by their own motivations, the mechanics refereed to move the story along); Preparing For Play (the lists - eight NPC names rolled on 1d8, the personality traits, the appearance characteristics; the coded notes - AC, HD, hp, MV, damage, the own maps and symbols, the fewer words the better; the THACO shorthand with the ogre example - 15 to hit AC 0, 9 against AC 6, 19 against AC -4; the map symbols; the anticipated surprises - steering back or expanding; the treasure decisions - the wealth, the balance impact, the matched challenge); and The Dungeon Master as Master Storyteller (the role most obvious during play; the pace - the minutes per melee and the story rate, the variety of intensity and rest, the discarded slow rules, the optional Weapons vs. AC and spell-component systems, the preparation, the pertinent-rules review; the voice - the tone of the tragic ruin and the jolly inn, the volume of the unexpected, the varied rate with the occasional pause; the colorful word choice - the door crashing inward in a blast of splinters; the NPC voices from the old men to the heroic leaders, augmented by the facial expressions and hand gestures) - the round ending at the HELP FROM THE PLAYERS head.

consts.comment: the NPC-name list: eight names provide most of the new NPCs encountered in a gaming session
consts.name: dcgNPCNameTable

consts.comment: the NPC-name roll: roll 1d8 (or select) from the list when someone is met
consts.name: dcgNPCNameDie

consts.comment: the THACO example: an ogre with 4+1 Hit Dice strikes an AC 0 opponent on a roll of 15 or better
consts.name: dcgOgreTHACO

bools.comment: a linear adventure advances through encounters that must be played in a certain order, the PCs given little or no choice between encounters
bools.name: dcgLinearDefines

bools.comment: dungeons work well for linear designs - a map leaving one possible route, each encounter planned with the PCs' predetermined locations known
bools.name: dcgLinearDungeons

bools.comment: outdoor linear adventures are harder to control, though thorn walls or impassable water occasionally limit PC choice
bools.name: dcgLinearOutdoor

bools.comment: the linear advantage: design time is never wasted on areas the PCs do not use
bools.name: dcgLinearNoWaste

bools.comment: linear design becomes harder as the PCs gain magical power - high-level mage and cleric spells defeat even dungeon corridors
bools.name: dcgLinearMagicPower

bools.comment: linear adventures work well for tournament play, all players meeting the same challenges
bools.name: dcgLinearTournament

bools.comment: for less structured play linear design is generally undesirable - players feel railroaded by the absence of choice
bools.name: dcgLinearUndesirable

bools.comment: directed play with the illusion of choice can succeed while actually being linear - players feel they control their own destiny
bools.name: dcgLinearIllusion

bools.comment: the open campaign de-emphasizes the DM's story, relying on PC choices; the DM's job is an interesting world to explore
bools.name: dcgOpenDefines

bools.comment: open-campaign preparation: detail the countryside all around and seed the entire area with conflicts so challenges are found wherever the PCs go
bools.name: dcgOpenPrep

bools.comment: open campaigns are fun especially for Adventurers - indefinite play plundering dungeons, stumbling into wars, discovering new worlds
bools.name: dcgOpenAdventurers

bools.comment: Problem-Solvers and Role-Players demand even more work - steady mental challenges and new unique NPCs; national-scope problems put rumors everywhere; nomadic NPCs are re-encountered
bools.name: dcgOpenMentalDiet

bools.comment: open campaigns demand great design time, but after enough adventures you have created and detailed an entire world setting
bools.name: dcgOpenWorldBuilding

bools.comment: the open campaign makes a structured story hard (exposition, development, climax); players may develop the structure themselves if clues lead them
bools.name: dcgOpenStoryHard

bools.comment: some players take perverse delight in the opposite of what you want; without reverse-psychology expertise a coherent story needs exceptional inventiveness
bools.name: dcgOpenPerverse

bools.comment: Events: encounters as events occur wherever the PCs are - place the dragon's lair in their path when wanted, with logic
bools.name: dcgOpenEvents

bools.comment: the time-management shortcut: ask players ahead what they feel like doing the next few sessions - general answers leave the details to you
bools.name: dcgOpenAskPlayers

bools.comment: large-scale background conflicts anchor the open campaign: wars (meeting the principals on each side) and disasters - the endless winter, the plague of man-eating plants - as continuing threads
bools.name: dcgOpenBackgroundConflicts

bools.comment: the matrix campaign allows a detailed story with developed plot while the players still choose where they go and how they deal with challenges
bools.name: dcgMatrixDefines

bools.comment: the key is a goal or series of goals the PCs are motivated to accomplish; a compromise between linear and open, effective for epics or strings of connecting stories
bools.name: dcgMatrixGoals

bools.comment: the matrix opening: a chosen location, a short exposition and clues opening options - the evil cleric sect with arrested peasants and raided temples
bools.name: dcgMatrixExposition

bools.comment: the next move is up to the players with guidance: the temple to the north, the great temple of good to the east, the peasants enslaved to the south - the headquarters to the west bided
bools.name: dcgMatrixGuidance

bools.comment: be prepared for a few courses of action: the temple raid, the sage interview, the prisoner rescue mission
bools.name: dcgMatrixPrepared

bools.comment: expand the matrix or point the clues toward the heart: the rescued prisoners led as an army, the good temple sending a quest for the item of great power
bools.name: dcgMatrixExpand

bools.comment: all the branches eventually steer the PCs toward the headquarters where the story's climax takes place
bools.name: dcgMatrixBranches

bools.comment: to move the plot along, schedule events wherever the PCs are: significant NPCs, visions and dreams, social or political changes, quick scenes showing a pertinent fact
bools.name: dcgMatrixPlotEvents

bools.comment: a matrix campaign must eventually meet a border beyond which the PCs are discouraged from passing - soft or hard
bools.name: dcgMatrixBorders

bools.comment: the soft border turns the PCs back through their own motivations: the hapless waifs appealing to decency, the mysterious stranger's gems for evidence of the sect's destruction
bools.name: dcgMatrixSoftBorder

bools.comment: the hard boundary for the unyielding: a cliff, stormy sea, or trackless desert, an army with escalating encounters; quest or geas spells only as a last resort
bools.name: dcgMatrixHardBorder

bools.comment: the matrix should hold several approaches to the final encounter and several means of dealing with it - never doomed for a wrong choice
bools.name: dcgMatrixMultiplePaths

bools.comment: prepare for players who have no idea what is going on: gently but firmly show the path - the henchman speaking up, the wise sage in plain language
bools.name: dcgMatrixLostPlayers

bools.comment: foreshadowing shows whether the PCs are on the right track - ill omens do not discourage but can indicate the way
bools.name: dcgMatrixForeshadowTrack

bools.comment: the DM's second responsibility begins at the table: presenting the story so the PCs are drawn in through their own motivations, and refereeing the mechanics so they move the story along rather than hinder it
bools.name: dcgRunningDefines

bools.comment: the more preparation time, the smoother the game; streamlining with lists when time is short
bools.name: dcgPrepSmoother

bools.comment: the random-generation lists: eight NPC names (roll 1d8), personality traits, and appearance characteristics - a ready-made expandable NPC generation system
bools.name: dcgPrepLists

bools.comment: the coded notes: AC, HD, hp, MV, and damage for encounters; your own maps and symbols for areas - the fewer words the better
bools.name: dcgPrepCodedNotes

bools.comment: THACO - To Hit Armor Class 0 - recorded per monster and NPC, frees you from consulting the combat tables during play; subtract the foe's AC from the THACO
bools.name: dcgPrepTHACO

bools.comment: develop map symbols for new location types - the more information on the map, the better the descriptions (the mapping section, p. 114)
bools.name: dcgPrepMapSymbols

bools.comment: anticipate unexpected PC actions: one or two surprises thought through can save the story line - steer the PCs back or expand the adventure in their direction
bools.name: dcgPrepSurprises

bools.comment: treasure placement decisions are too important for the last minute: the wealth placed, the magic items' impact on balance, the challenge matched to the value
bools.name: dcgPrepTreasure

bools.comment: the storyteller role is most obvious during play: describing settings, running the many NPCs, springing dramatic surprises - the listeners' involvement drives it home
bools.name: dcgStorytellerDefines

bools.comment: storytelling improves by applying proven principles, incorporated with no advance preparation
bools.name: dcgStorytellerPrinciples

bools.comment: pace affects both game mechanics and story development - the minutes per melee and the story rate are functions of pace, under the DM's great control
bools.name: dcgPaceDefines

bools.comment: pace variety: moments of dramatic suspense and intensity broken by periods of rest and security for discussing options and making plans
bools.name: dcgPaceVariety

bools.comment: discard rules that significantly slow the pace - streamlined versions or simple DM decree
bools.name: dcgPaceDiscardRules

bools.comment: Weapons vs. Armor Class Modifications and detailed spell-component recording suit detail-lovers; role-playing-centered players may proceed smoothly without them
bools.name: dcgPaceOptionalSystems

bools.comment: preparation gives pace control - detailed notes prevent wasted thought during the game and snap decisions that destroy the campaign's balance
bools.name: dcgPacePreparation

bools.comment: review the pertinent rules before critical situations: a complicated new monster, or a watery environment's swimming and boating rules
bools.name: dcgPaceRulesReview

bools.comment: voice is the DM's primary tool - information, mood, and the emotions of surprise, anger, triumph, and fear; tone, volume, rate, and word choice
bools.name: dcgVoicePrimary

bools.comment: tone conveys many emotions best: the aura of sadness for the tragically abandoned ruin, the laughter and jolliness of the friendly inn
bools.name: dcgVoiceTone

bools.comment: volume conveys the sudden and shocking, but beware overdoing it - a loud outburst is only effective if unexpected
bools.name: dcgVoiceVolume

bools.comment: vary the rate of speech for intensity - the occasional pause lets listeners absorb an impact or ponder the unknown
bools.name: dcgVoiceRate

bools.comment: colorful word choice through practice and reading - 'The door crashes inward in a blast of splinters!'; written passages read aloud before use
bools.name: dcgWordChoice

bools.comment: develop a variety of NPC voices - old men, women, children, witches, pirates, greedy merchants, suspicious guards, gloating villains, heroic leaders - augmented by facial expressions and hand gestures
bools.name: dcgNPCVoices

examples.note: the NPC list: eight names, rolled on 1d8.

the THACO arithmetic: AC 6 hit on 9, AC -4 hit on 19.

the matrix: the soft and hard borders.
